parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French ambre, from Old French ambre, from Arabic عَنْبَر (ʕanbar, “ambergris”), from Middle Persian ʾmbl (ambar, “ambergris”).
From either Arabic حَشَّاشِين (ḥaššāšīn, “hashish users”) or أَسَاسِيُّون (ʔasāsiyyūn).
Borrowed from Arabic عَادَة (ʕāda, “habit, wont, custom, usage, practice”).
Borrowed from Arabic أَبُو حِبَاب (ʔabū ḥibāb, “fruit of many seeds”).

parole.significato: horse-armour, also a long saddle for an ass or mule of canvas, pack-saddle
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French barde, through Arabic بَرْدَة (barda); ultimately from Middle Persian pltk' (pardag). Compare to Persian پرده (parde), Old Armenian պարտակ (partak), and Classical Syriac ܦܪܕܩܐ (pardəqā).
From brik, itself from an Arabic word borrowed from Ottoman Turkish بورك (börek).
Borrowed into Old French bedoïns from Arabic بَدَوِيّ (badawiyy).

From Arabic بَنِي (banī, “sons of”) + oui oui, thus roughly “the tribe of yes-yes”. Originally referred disparagingly to the Muslim advisers employed by the French in colonial northern Africa, many of whom were servile and therefore ineffective.
Borrowed from Arabic بَازَهْر (bāzahr, “bezoar”), ultimately from Middle Persian pʾtzhl (pādzahr, “antidote, bezoar”).

parole.significato: qadi (civil judge in certain Islamic countries)

parole.significato: Sha'ban (the eighth month of the Islamic calendar)

shakshuka (dish of eggs simmered in a mixture of vegetables and spices)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic خِلَاف (ḵilāf) (spoken in Egyptian Arabic something like /xaˈlæːf/).

parole.significato: Shawwal (the tenth month of the Islamic calendar)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic شَبَكَة (šabaka, “net”), after the net-like structure of the wadis.

parole.significato: lookout (person on watch for approaching enemy, police, danger, etc.)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic كُسْكُس (kuskus), from a Berber language.
From crouillat (which has the same meaning), from a Maghrebi Arabic word meaning "brother". Ultimately from Arabic أخ (ʔaḵ, literally “brother”).

parole.significato: a decree issued by the king of Morocco
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic ظَهِير (ẓahīr), via Moroccan Arabic

parole.significato: hyrax (any species of the order Hyracoidea)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic دَمَان (إِسْرَائِيل) (damān (ʔisrāʔīl), literally “lamb (of Israel)”).

parole.significato: fatwa (legal opinion issued by a mufti)

Borrowed from Arabic فُنْدُق (funduq), borrowed from Ancient Greek πανδοκεῖον (pandokeîon), from πᾰν- (păn-, “all, every”) + δοκ- (dok-, o-grade of the stem of δέχομαι (dékhomai, “to receive”)) + -εῖον (-eîon).

parole.significato: Gazan (of or from Gaza or the Gaza Strip)

Borrowed from Arabic حَامٍ (ḥāmin) or حَمِيّ (ḥamiyy).

parole.significato: sepulchral chamber in a rock mass, hypogeum

Borrowed from Arabic حَشِيش (ḥašīš, “hay, dried herb”).
Borrowed from Arabic حَسّ (ḥass) (in spite of the gender difference, which in French or Indo-European follows abstract meanings or comparable meanings being of feminine gender).
Borrowed from Arabic حَشُومَة (ḥašūma). Compare Dutch hsjoema.

Borrowed from Arabic اِنْتِفَاضَة (intifāḍa, “shaking off, uprising, insurrection”).
Inherited from Old French jare, from Arabic جَرَّة (jarra, “earthen receptacle”).
From Arabic قَبَائِل (qabāʔil, “tribes”), plural of قَبِيلَة (qabīla, “tribe”).

From a Maghrebi form of Arabic قَصْر (qaṣr).

From Middle French lache (“resinous material”), borrowed from Arabic لكّ (“lacquer”).
Frequently until the nineteenth century lilac, borrowed in the seventeenth from Arabic لِيلَك (līlak).

From Arabic مُورْتَاز (mūrtāz, “fastened”), from رَازَا (rāzā, “to cut a recess”).

Borrowed from Arabic صَحْرَاوِيّ (ṣaḥrāwiyy, “of the desert”, from صَحْرَاء (ṣaḥrāʔ, “desert”)).

From Arabic سُعُودِيّ (suʕūdiyy). By surface analysis, Saoud + -i.
From earlier sarbatane, sarbatanne by connection with canne (“stick”), from Arabic سَبَطَانَة (sabaṭāna).
From dialectal Arabic سْلُوڭِي (slūgī, “greyhound”), from Arabic سَلُوقِيّ (salūqiyy, “greyhound”). See also English Saluki.

Probably from Arabic سِحْر (siḥr, “witchcraft, magic, charm”).

From Arabic طِلَّسْم (ṭillasm), from Ancient Greek τέλεσμα (télesma, “payment”).

Borrowed from Arabic تَفّ (taff). Synonym of pouah.

Inherited from Middle French and Old French emir, from Arabic أَمِير (ʔamīr).
Inherited from Old French bourrache, from Medieval Latin borāgō or borrago, either from Latin borra (“short wool, rough hair”) or Arabic أَبُو العَرَق (ʔabū l-ʕaraq, literally “father of sweat”).

parole.significato: zucchetto (skullcap worn by Roman Catholic clergy)

Borrowed from Arabic حَسّ (ḥass) or from Arabic حسد.
